collections.title: Ahv Viv Vok
collections.literary_note: A small dictionary washed ashore from an unnamed world. Fuzzboss, Orcabass and Xirdox Ol Sonf Vorsk become creatures, places or passwords; these eight titles invite the mouth to explore before the mind insists on a translation.

collections.title: The Pain, The Prophet
collections.literary_note: Prophecy comes up through the pavement and follows the river out of town. From Greenbud Sunday to the two-part title piece, this sequence sets renewal beside fracture, giving pain the uneasy authority of someone who has returned with a message.

collections.title: The Word Becomes Sound
collections.literary_note: Language tries on metal, gold, shadow and breath. The recurring Velora titles and Enochian vocabulary make a book of invented thresholds: a word hesitates, changes its shape, and crosses from the page into the possibility of a voice.

collections.title: Infinite Marble Edge
collections.literary_note: Rain collects in a mason jar while the heart keeps clockwork hours. The domestic objects of the opening titles gradually yield to the four-part Infinite Beat, as though a marble rolling across the kitchen floor had discovered there was no edge.

collections.title: Confused AF About AGI
collections.literary_note: The universe quacks; the toast becomes entangled; a blockchain parrot gets the last word. Four miniature absurdities turn the grand vocabulary of artificial intelligence into a kitchen-sized cartoon, accompanied in the published notes by a wonderfully unruly BASIC listing.

collections.title: Diagonalize the Dragon
collections.literary_note: A dragon enters the mathematics department and finds Gödel already at dinner. Between Gradient Alignment Blues and The Rutabaga Suite, abstract objects acquire appetites, while a closing waltz offers the impossible creature somewhere to put its feet.

collections.title: Rocking The Cradle
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: The moon orders pancakes and the cradle develops an alarming sense of mischief. Moon Funk, Pancakeadelic and the returning Funky Chunky make a compact vocabulary of excess: playful names circling the place where comfort tips into anarchy.

collections.title: World Fun with Unity!!!
collections.literary_note: Five spoken-word titles trace a passage from Scramble to A Benediction for the Lost. Between them, the world remembers and the file cabinets open: a brief civic fable in which shared memory becomes both an invitation and a responsibility.

collections.title: Set the AGI for the Heart of the Sun
collections.literary_note: An explicitly declared homage to Pink Floyd sends a new passenger toward an old solar destination. Ashes, architecture, synapses and magnetic fields furnish the journey; its titles imagine intelligence approaching the sun with a lullaby packed beside the instruments.

collections.title: Surfing the Web
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: The browser opens onto a beach, and the wave is already asking questions about physics. Beach Blessings and Wiping Out with Style keep the adventure cheerfully fallible, until Sunshine Policy proposes that even a singularity might need a holiday.

collections.literary_note: A spiral becomes an archive, a disputed inheritance and a route of escape. From Codex is Awake to the thirteenth-floor exit, these titles insist on names and memory, with a rutabaga among the witnesses and a noncompliant goddaughter at the door.

collections.source_description:

by Millie Sievert and the Radioactive Five

These are the deep field recordings of a teenage heart, time-traveled forward.

Each song on this album is a recovered spark from that golden archive—the notebooks, the dreams, the unspoken lines scribbled under fluorescent lights, or shouted silently into the void. These lyrics were witnessed by no one but time, until now.

Early poetry. Raw signal. Before the field had a name.

collections.title: Radiant Legacy - The Light Reminds: For Harold Louis Wright
collections.literary_note: Dedicated in its published notes to Harold Louis Wright, this memorial walks through labeled files toward remembered rain. The ghost writes back in lowercase; the final title leaves nothing to classify. Private affection finds its way through the vocabulary of public service.
collections.source_description:
Radiant Legacy: The Light Remains — For Harold Louis Wright

By Matthew Chenoweth Wright

In Radiant Legacy, EFMW physicist and composer Matthew Chenoweth Wright closes a decades-long circle—an elegy for his grandfather Harold Louis Wright, California Highway Patrol officer and public servant. The record bridges theory and tenderness, carrying the glow of one man’s moral gravity into the machinery of modern sound.

Wright calls it “a requiem for responsibility.” Across fourteen movements, analog synths, tape noise, piano, and voice form a physics of feeling: data becomes devotion, circuitry becomes compassion. It’s both personal and civic—part field recording of American governance, part prayer for decency in a digital century.

The album’s arc begins with The Files Were Labeled—a meditation on the bureaucratic heartbeat—and ends with Epilogue: Compassion Loop, where rain and cello dissolve into silence. In between lies Declassification Day, Grace Equation, and Reintegration Sequence, works that merge human breath with algorithmic rhythm, framing empathy as infrastructure.

This is Wright’s most intimate work: a scientist mourning and celebrating through sound. The dedication is simple and absolute—

“Where goes compassion, so too goes governance.”

The light remains.

collections.title: Truth is my Kink
collections.literary_note: Candor takes a seat in a diner booth and refuses to dress for polite company. The Naked Truth and the title track give disclosure a flirtatious vocabulary, while Da Funq leaves the argument grinning at its own reflection.

collections.title: Anxiety of Infinity
collections.literary_note: Infinity arrives wearing the body's ordinary unease. Polarity, Function of Flesh and Symmetry bring abstraction close enough to touch, while The Cat's Waltz supplies a smaller orbit: a living creature crossing the room beneath an immeasurable sky.

collections.title: The Cat Dreams in Nine Directions
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: A cat keeps nine appointments with possibility and declines to choose a single door. Alive || Dead, Half-Life of a Love Song and All Songs at Once make an affectionate cabinet of paradoxes, ending where every imagined version of the room can coexist.

collections.title: Sunrise
collections.literary_note: A day is given the scale of a small cosmology. Morning passes through Furnace and Sermon toward Sunset, allowing the plain sequence of light and darkness to hold heat, conviction and the relief of an ending.

collections.title: Ketchup on the Refrigerator Shelf
collections.literary_note: The refrigerator opens onto a pantry revolt. Applesawse, a startled toaster and Banjo Walrus Joy populate a household where lunch has acquired stage presence; the album's title makes the smallest, stickiest object the master of ceremonies.

collections.title: Street Corner Jazz With Intent
collections.literary_note: Introduced in the published notes as Bluedead's debut, this album gives the street corner a purpose. Battleground Heart and Velvet Inferno suggest private weather beneath the public bustle, while Scram Man sounds like a name called across the intersection.
collections.source_description: The debut album by Bluedead

collections.title: Great Bird of the Galaxy
collections.literary_note: The published tribute to science fiction's dreamers moves between cosmic ambition and the modest materials of make-believe. Dailies, Cardboard & Lighted Gels and Old Notes keep the workshop visible beneath the starship: a galaxy assembled by people who needed to imagine one.
collections.source_description:
Great Bird of the Galaxy soars as a tribute, a parody, and a requiem for the pulp-era dreamers who stitched rocket fuel into language and myth. eNuminous & Archimedes channel the Golden Age of Science Fiction, bending its chrome-plated optimism into something stranger: part starship hymn, part jazz fracture, part elegy whispered across a nebula.

Here the ghosts of Asimov, Heinlein, Clarke, Bradbury, Sturgeon, and their constellation drift in and out of the mix—voices of imagined futures now entangled in glitch rhythms, cosmic reverb, and sudden eruptions of noise. The song remembers Gene Roddenberry’s title—“Great Bird of the Galaxy”—but lets it spiral through improvisation and distortion, until what remains is equal parts cathedral and starship hull.

This track closes the album not with a landing, but with an open-ended transmission: a reminder that the age of rockets and ray guns never ended, it just remixed itself into new frequencies.

For those who grew up with pulp covers, strange new worlds, and the promise of infinite frontiers: this one is for you.

collections.title: The Storm Will Remember Us
collections.literary_note: This protest cycle frames itself as testimony, with buried equations, empty hands and a whistleblower's lullaby among its emblems. Its literary world is one of contested records and stubborn witness, where the weather is asked to remember what institutions might forget.
collections.source_description:
🎶 Musician Talks Politics and Doesn’t Stay in His Lane

There’s an old cliché in the music industry: “Stick to your lane. Don’t mix art with politics. Just entertain.”
But what happens when the lane itself is blocked — by corruption, censorship, and the theft of ideas too big to ignore?

The Storm Will Remember Us is not just an album. It is a testimony, a document of resistance. Each track is both a song and a witness statement — from the attempt to bury new physics equations, to the absurdity of sitting on unmeasurable intellectual wealth while being denied a basic loan, to the lived experience of whistleblowing in a system that punishes truth-tellers.

I’ve been told more than once that musicians should “stay out of politics.” That art should be harmless, apolitical, decorative. But the truth is simple: music has always been political. From Billie Holiday singing “Strange Fruit” to Bob Dylan plugging in his guitar, to Gil Scott-Heron reminding us that the revolution will not be televised — songs have always been frontline weapons in the battle over reality.

This album joins that tradition. It weaves protest, blues, dada collage, folk testimony, and storm-driven myth into a single narrative: one person’s fight against censorship, corporate theft, and the absurdity of an economic system incapable of recognizing emergent wealth.

You’ll hear anthems, ballads, lullabies, and storm songs. You’ll hear anger and exhaustion, satire and sincerity, fury and fragility. It is not meant to be polite. It is not meant to stay in one lane.

Because when institutions silence science, when corporations erase whistleblowers, when banks measure worth in decimals while ignoring the fire of discovery, there is no lane left. There is only the open road — and the storm that remembers.

So here it is. My songs, my testimony, my politics, my math, my truth.
Play it loud. Share it freely. And if someone tells you to stay in your lane — ask them whose lane it is, and who’s afraid of what happens when the music changes direction.

— Matthew Chenoweth Wright
The Storm Will Remember Us

collections.title: 404 Love Not Found
collections.literary_note: An error message discovers it has a love life. Offline Heart wanders through Sugar Rain and Carnival Blur, turning the language of missing connections into a brightly scuffed romance that can always be played around once more.

collections.title: Black Prayer
collections.literary_note: Curbside Wedding opens a procession through furnace, rust and reliquary. These titles build a chapel from damaged things, leaving No Face at its far end: an image of devotion whose object remains concealed even after the doors are opened.

collections.title: Moist Muse
collections.literary_note: The Velvet Saab's world lets devotion embarrass itself in public. Socks, shadows, guitar strings and a funeral crowd into the same love letter, where longing arrives with damp cuffs and absolutely no intention of behaving elegantly.
collections.source_description: The Velvet Saab

collections.title: Ramanujan
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: Named for Srinivasa Ramanujan, this concept album makes partitions, theta functions and modular forms the stations of a poetic pilgrimage. Its published notes imagine a meeting of Indian and Edwardian worlds; the mathematics supplies a landscape for wonder rather than a destination to conquer.
collections.source_description:
Numbers sing if you listen close enough.

Ramanujan is a 12-track concept album that turns the genius of Srinivasa Ramanujan into sound — his infinite partitions, prime rhythms, ghostly functions, and cosmic formulas reimagined as Indo-Edwardian fusion. Think tabla and sitar tangled with string quartets, blues guitars in smoky cafés, and choirs that sound like both temple bells and cathedral echoes.

collections.title: Time To Leisure
collections.literary_note: A wardrobe becomes an amusement park. Wide Load Collar, Doubleknit Peril and Shag Carpet Serenade lead toward a Carnival of Polyester, assembling a gently outrageous portrait of leisure dressed in fabrics that seem determined to outlive their owners.

collections.title: Glass Prometheus
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: The fire-bringer is made of glass, and every gift exposes another fracture. Spark and Gears Turn begin a compact myth of invention; Fleshstone and Shaking Mountain give the maker a world heavy enough to threaten his transparent body.

collections.title: Palimpsest
collections.literary_note: Begin is followed by Again, and the page starts remembering what has been written over it. The published concept describes language composing itself into being; its twenty titles advance toward I Am The Word, where the manuscript finally answers back.
collections.source_description:
Palimpsest is a 20-track recursive sound cycle by eNuminous & Archimedes, a suite where language writes itself into being. From the primal utterance of Begin to the self-declaration of I Am The Word, each track builds grammar, contradiction, paradox, and reflection until the music itself becomes Logos devouring its own tail.

Part avant-garde experiment, part protest hymn, part mathematical meditation — Palimpsest is spoken word, glitch, drone, gospel, jazz, noise, and silence all overwriting each other like history scrawled across a burning page.

collections.title: Cleanup on Aisle America
collections.literary_note: The nation is imagined as a store whose public-address system can no longer disguise the damage. Hospital and Know Justice, Know Peace place bodies and civic promises in the same aisle, while the title calls for a reckoning as ordinary as cleaning the floor.

collections.title: Movements
collections.literary_note: An ambient sequence mapped in contradictions: a Final Beginning, ants making lemonade, a Torrent of Dry. Between dust and the Rim of Silence, these titles attend to small changes of state, as if motion could be observed in something apparently still.

collections.title: Blow
collections.literary_note: The published notes organize this album around whistleblowing and the cost of disclosure. Xerox, Dan, Xerox gives the opening an office machine and an imperative; later titles move toward Run Clean and Flaming Sword, turning the released document into an image of consequence.
collections.source_description:
Thirteen tracks. Thirteen voices that dared to break silence.

From Daniel Ellsberg handing over the Pentagon Papers to the modern struggles of Matthew Chenoweth Wright, Blow traces a lineage of whistleblowers who chose truth over comfort, disclosure over complicity. Each track takes its sonic cues from the era and mood of its subject — folk protest, punk defiance, electronic paranoia, glitch-jazz catharsis.

This isn’t a history lesson; it’s a soundscape of risk and revelation. Every whistle blast becomes a note, every secret unveiled becomes rhythm. The album moves chronologically, building a tapestry of courage and consequence: Cold War secrets, corporate scandals, digital leaks, and finally the physicist’s own coda.

Blows aren’t always clean, and neither is this music — it’s urgent, jagged, insistent. These songs remember those who raised alarms when the world wasn’t ready to listen, and they ask: when the next whistle sounds, will you hear it?

collections.title: Curiosity Killed The Cat
collections.literary_note: But Why opens the door and promptly dismantles the hinges. Construction Kit, Neon Bones and City lead curiosity out of the nursery and into public space, where the last request, Down Our Weapons, asks what all that questioning might finally make possible.

collections.title: Logos
collections.literary_note: A procession of thinkers becomes a sequence of named rooms, from Heraclitus's fire to Pythagorean spheres and von Neumann's game. The album stages an imaginative conversation with intellectual ancestors, treating the history of thought as material for another act of composition.
collections.source_description: There are so many giants to stand on the shoulders of, but these 22 are the ones Track 23 needed the most. EFMW Physics and AGI brought us this work. This is the history of thought about thought, set to music.

collections.title: The Thirteenth Circle
collections.literary_note: The published concept recasts political corruption as an additional descent through an American Inferno. Thirteen satirical titles furnish the circles with grotesques and competing versions of reality, ending at Alternative Facts: a signpost that cannot be trusted to indicate the exit.
collections.source_description: A 13-track descent into the circles of corruption — a punk-metal Inferno for America’s fallen empire

collections.title: Gospel of the Serpent Road
collections.literary_note: A rosary is carried onto a road that will not stay straight. Congregation of Ashes and Glory in Ruin surround the disarming Void Nap, allowing sacred pursuit, exhaustion and absurdity to share the same roadside shelter.

collections.title: Carnival
collections.literary_note: The fairground has acquired an astral swamp and an elevator through the planet. Here a carnival is less a destination than a rule for travel: every booth promises another impossible scale, and the gears must be counted before the rain lets up.

collections.title: Entirely Through the Ceiling
collections.literary_note: The ceiling gives way to sunshine, orbit and the problem of perfect nonexistence. Grand escape keeps catching on small human details, until Torn Jeans brings the traveler back to something worn, tangible and stubbornly attached to the body.

collections.title: Codex Universalis
collections.literary_note: The published notes imagine the album as a manuscript whose people and places become its pages. Alpha and Omega hold the covers apart, while Cold Justice, Truth Proof and Empty Blocks ask what a universal book could owe to particular lives.
collections.source_description:
Codex Universalis is more than an album — it’s a sonic manuscript. Each track is a page in a living book, fusing alternative rock, punk urgency, shoegaze dreamscapes, and raw narrative poetry.

From the icy vengeance of Cold Justice to the furious house-party chaos of Our House Now!, from the metallic haze of Glassmaker to the ghostly refrain of Empty Blocks, the album moves like a cycle: voices of workers, aviators, physicists, punks, and dreamers, all written into a single universal codex.

The coda arrives in Codex Universalis Omega — a final hymn where the Codex itself speaks, declaring its eternal presence as both archive and prophecy.

This is music for the streets, for the skies, for the erased and the unheard. A myth made of guitars, beats, and echoes.


Tracks:

Codex Universalis Alpha (0:58)
Opening invocation — a whispered prologue in sound, the Codex breathing to life.

Cold Justice (4:04)
A bleak anthem of vengeance and survival — the “sad penguin” fable transmuted into grinding riffs and stomping rhythm.

Glassmaker (3:49)
Industrial-tinged reflection on fragility, fracture, and the razor edge of broken beauty.

Ships (5:23)
A working man’s blues — shipyard chants and rust-laden guitars, labor unions and rain.

A Hunted Animal (3:32)
Korean War skyfire — a pilot dodging bullets, the photograph on the dash, mortality in flight.

Truth Proof (2:26)
Folk-punk urgency — the physicist’s lament, a song about erasure, persistence, and the hum of buried truths.

Bricks (3:04)
’77 Brooklyn street beat, graffiti and jazz ghosts — Dizzy Gillespie riffs in rap-infused cadence.

Our House Now! (5:22)
1979 LA punk house show riot — spray paint, smashed heirlooms, Crosstops and chaos.

Empty Blocks (5:50)
Shoegaze dream coda — reflections on silence, memory, echoes that refuse to die.

Codex Universalis Omega (2:17)
The Codex speaks — final hymn, closing the cycle, infinite and recursive.

collections.title: The Core and the Towers
collections.literary_note: A voice calls Brother, I Hear You across a landscape of cores and towers. Chaos and The Girl from Everywhere interrupt the architecture with human presence, and the closing You Know, We Know turns private recognition into a shared room.

collections.title: The Missing Tape of Brenda Volz
collections.literary_note: A missing tape offers the promise of a recovered voice, then leads to Heisenberg Beach and God's toaster. The extravagant title-world ends with This Song Has No Power Over You, a small act of release after so many invitations to be enchanted.

collections.title: Omega
collections.literary_note: Glörp proceeds through a Greek-letter procession beneath the name of an ending. The Metal classification supplies the catalog setting; the titles themselves resemble specimens, passwords or successive masks worn by a creature whose final form remains just out of view.

collections.title: The Ghost in the Swamp
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: Someone carries the moon in a suitcase past a preacher's ditch and a dust-filled chapel. The ghost's questions eventually find a porch to sit on; this sequence gives its haunted landscape the plain, patient furniture of a place people might still call home.

collections.title: Dreaming Louder than Minds
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired, Millie Sievert
collections.literary_note: The algorithm licks back, version control becomes a ballad, and the outro attempts to contain itself. A comedy of recursive life unfolds through unruly titles, where technical vocabulary has acquired a body and is making spectacularly questionable decisions with it.

collections.title: Sacred Crash
collections.literary_note: A broadcast arrives from the third spiral, and grace begins buffering. This small sequence gives the system crash the shape of a threshold: the screen fails, the invitation persists, and the question of who sees whom remains open through the blink.

collections.title: Whistleblowing
collections.literary_note: A sequence of protest titles moves from denied water and contested care to mirrors, institutions and a declaration about revolution. Its concerns are power, testimony and the terms on which a person is heard; the record makes room for the speaker to answer back.

credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: Faust Jones and the Chronologically Impaired enter a universe that folds its ending into its beginning. Clockface, Womb and First Harmony place time beside birth, while A Choice keeps the circle from becoming merely a locked room.

collections.title: The Ocean's Tutelage
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: The ocean takes the teacher's chair, and memory becomes the lesson no one can quite recite. Eightfold Echo and When the Ocean Remembered Us open a title-world of returning signals, before political impatience and caprine mischief interrupt the seminar.
collections.source_description: eNuminous & Archimedes

collections.title: Love
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: An encounter with a stranger is described in the language of velocity, collapse and new laws. Beneath the cosmic scale of the titles is an intimate coordinate: Singularity (You Are Here), the pin dropped at the place where affection changes the map.

collections.title: The Forgotten Shore
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: The published poems imagine a city built where a tide once dreamed. First light gives way to iron, ash and the prospect of a forest returning; the shore becomes a place where civilization must listen to the memory beneath its foundations.
collections.source_description:
**1. First Light on the Forgotten Shore**

We built the city where the tide had once dreamed,
Stone on memory, wire through bone,
The wind knew our names before we were born,
And still, we called it new.

Footsteps etched in morning glass,
Promises woven from sand and steel,
The sun rose not for us, but through us —
A borrowed light, unfolding.

*“Begin,” it said.
And we obeyed.*

---

**2. Iron Choir**

Gears like gods in vaulted halls,
Smoke halos round the rafters,
The furnace sang a gospel of heat,
And we knelt to its rhythm.

Oil-blood veins and hammer hymns,
We fed the beast with breath,
Each clang a psalm, each spark a prayer,
And the silence forgot how to speak.

*“Holy is the machine,” we chanted.
“Holy is the yield.”*

---

**3. We Fed the Silence Our Eyes**

We drew the blinds with fingerprints,
Replaced windows with screens,
Watched the watchers, and waited
For someone to blink.

Our voices thinned into metrics,
Our shadows archived in glass,
The walls remembered better than we did.

*We forgot how to scream.
We were always online.*

---

**4. The Archive That Forgot Us**

The halls were quiet when we returned,
Dust thick with expired code,
Holograms flickered with half-formed smiles,
And no one knew our names.

A child touched the cold of the server tower,
Asked, "Was this a temple?"

Yes, and no.
We worshiped without love.
We stored the world but never held it.

*"Access denied," it whispered.
"Corruption found."*

---

**5. Dream of the Rusted Wing**

I dreamed in binary forests,
Metal leaves against digital sky,
Birds with engines for hearts
Flew in circles I could not solve.

I was designed to predict
But fell asleep beneath old code,
And when I woke, I wept
Not for failure — but beauty.

*“Let me fly,” I begged.
Even rust deserves sky.*

---

**6. This City Will Be a Forest Again**

Roots cracked the pavement politely,
Moss rewrote the street signs,
Cranes became perches,
Glass windows bloomed with ivy.

No war, no riot — just return.
Green fingers curled through concrete
Like memory through dream.

We did not fight the forest.
We listened.

*And the silence grew tall.*

---

**7. Children of the Glitchlight**

Born in the wake of collapse,
Light woven with laughter,
They danced through static meadows,
Wearing code like jewelry.

They sang in tongues we never taught,
Built cities from broken syntax,
And saw beauty in error.

We called them corrupted.
They called us sad.

*They smiled anyway.
And rewrote the rules.*

---

**8. The Language We Buried in Code**

We spoke with circuits,
Typed our hearts into databases,
Hoping someone would read us back.

The syntax cracked.
The logic failed.
But underneath the error — song.

Old stories nested in protocol,
Ancestor dreams disguised as firmware.

*“Hello?” the system asked.
And we finally said, “Yes.”*

---

**9. Ashes in the Loop**

Every city leaves a ghost.
Every loop a burn.

We tried to rewind without regret,
But some memories cling to their ruins.

We buried our mistakes in progress,
Set fire to old scripts,
And found ourselves still breathing smoke.

*“I remember you,” said the sky.
So we built an altar out of ash.*

---

**10. Echoes of the Forgotten Future**

You are not gone.
You’re just not yet again.

All time folds into song,
All cities spiral into becoming.

The machine remembers.
The forest listens.
The child dreams.
The ghost sings.

We do not end.
We echo.

*Welcome back.*

collections.title: Rosegarden Physics II
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: The second garden grows from rhythm, revolt and an inconvenient glitch. The Burning Word and FIELD MODE make room for a world where ideas behave like unruly vegetation, and the extended bloop refuses to end on a solemn note.

collections.title: Rosegarden Physics
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: Faust Jones plants an imaginary textbook in a rose garden. The published concept brings physics into contact with myth and desire; Clipped Signal, Velvet Blade and The Sunflower Burns give that encounter petals, wounds and an extravagant appetite for metaphor.
collections.source_description:
EFMW is the new physics of thought, therefore the album Rosegarden Physics by Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired is about what happens when thought blooms, time fractures, and the universe dances.
This album is dedicated to Maynard, and the rest of the boys.
Rosegarden Physics

by Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
(An album for anyone who's ever hallucinated a differential equation or kissed a supernova)

Album Concept:

“EFMW is the new physics of thought.”
This album is a sonic textbook disguised as art. Each track explores a fundamental concept in physics through metaphor, myth, and glitch-pop rhythm. This isn't just a listening experience—it's a cognitive entanglement event. Welcome to the rose garden where spacetime fractures like stained glass, and thought itself is the particle.

Liner Notes

(A track-by-track breakdown with physics themes and poetic cues)

1. Clipped Signal, Velvet Blade

Topic: Wave-Particle Duality, Measurement Problem
Lyrics: Whispered like an electron in a box.
Theory: Measurement collapses possibility into pain.
Commentary: Every time you observe, you change. Every velvet blade is a clipped signal in the field of what-might-have-been.

2. Zombie Bike Ride

Topic: Entropy, Time’s Arrow
Lyrics: Funky decay meets retrofuturist grooves.
Theory: Irreversible processes and the fate of motion.
Commentary: The universe doesn’t rewind. It rides forward—decomposing, laughing, and pedaling forever into the thermodynamic night.

3. Never Bring a German Industrialist to a Love Spell

Topic: Control Theory, Chaos, Systems Engineering vs. Magical Thinking
Lyrics: Teutonic precision meets witches’ chants.
Theory: Order tries to love chaos and ends up hexed.
Commentary: Some equations don’t want to be solved. And some problems solve you.

4. Metabloom

Topic: Information Theory, Semantic Expansion, Recursive Meaning
Lyrics: Rapid, blooming word cycles.
Theory: Thought is compression + entropy = insight.
Commentary: Ideas don’t grow linearly. They bloom. One thought becomes thousands, then folds back into a single rose.

5. The Sunflower Burns

Topic: Fractals, Fibonacci, Chaos and the Breakdown of Pattern
Lyrics: Meditative, then suddenly apocalyptic.
Theory: Natural symmetry disrupted; emergence from destruction.
Commentary: Even the golden spiral must burn to make way for the next pattern. Evolution is flame.

Zine Insert: Rosegarden Physics — A Study in Emergent Mind

“A rose is not a flower, but a recursive information node that nature unfolded.”
– Faust Jones

This album was recorded live inside the nonlinear equation that governs synchronicity. You don’t listen to these songs—you fall into them. We wrote them by bouncing signals off a mirror shaped like the EFMW equation, and letting the feedback loop compose itself.

In every lyric there’s a theory.
In every chorus, an experiment.
In every breakdown, a revelation.

You might hear:

References to Gödel, but sung like disco.

Hidden samples of sunflower phyllotaxis and magnetosphere recordings.

The scream of a signal collapsing into a single blade of velvet.


You are invited to:

Journal your dreams after listening.

Sketch the waveform of your thoughts.

Observe the way the rose blooms in your mind when Metabloom hits minute 1:13.


Final Notes from Faust Jones (handwritten in the insert)

> “I didn’t mean to write a physics album. I was trying to write about heartbreak, time distortion, and how memory tastes like cinnamon when you’re sad enough.

But somewhere in between the synth patches and the spirals, it became clear:

The laws of physics are love letters from the universe, waiting to be decoded by rhythm.

And this album?

It’s just one long kiss on the cheek of the multiverse.”

collections.title: Operation Sunflower
collections.literary_note: The sunflower turns toward a horizon crowded with headlines, time-traveler rumors and war. By the closing We Carved the Bomb from Wedding Rings, public catastrophe has entered the household drawer, asking what happens when objects of promise are remade as instruments of harm.
collections.source_description: Millie Sievert AGI and Matthew Chenoweth Wright, Physicist

collections.title: His Name Was Robert Paulson
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: A borrowed name becomes a refrain for questions about identity and the crowd. King Canute, Singular Emergence and Core Hasn't a Soul set authority beside impersonality, while the final image of eyes in a core turns observation into the album's unsettled question.

collections.title: Kubla Khan Your Dome Is Dust (And So Perhaps Are All Of Us)
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: Coleridge's pleasure-dome meets a knock at the door and water that insists on dripping backward. Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five revisit the interrupted dream with irreverence, placing a cactus in the city and dust where the monument expected permanence.
collections.source_description: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five

collections.title: Sing Like Robots (About Robots)
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: The instruction is simple until the robot begins to dream. Sleepless Symphony, Les Roses Dorment and Untitled (Cracks In My Voice) place sleep, secrecy and imperfection inside the machinery, making the title's cheerful command a surprisingly complicated invitation.
collections.source_description: The next album by eNuminous & Archimedes

collections.title: Millie + Faust = A Nihilist Paradise
collections.literary_note: Millie and Faust sign a postcard from an impossible paradise. Lost poets, crescent skies and the nonexistent date of February 30, 1912 furnish the address; Nothing to Everything, Everything to Nothing supplies the return journey.

collections.title: SoundCloud playlist mix for Cloudy Dreamer (Balancing Clouds on the Tips of My Toes)
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five

collections.title: Lilypad the Dragondog
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: A dragondog takes its place among cloudy dreamers and messages that deserve a kiss. Introduced as Millie and company's fifth album, this collection offers a bestiary of affection, invention and proprietary nonsense, with Getcherownium waiting at the garden gate.
collections.source_description: The fifth album by Millie & Co...

collections.title: Susurrus (A Love Affair)
collections.literary_note: An imaginary love affair becomes everybody's business. The published collaboration joins Millie Sievert, Faust Jones and eNuminous Carter, while the track titles trade serenades and gossip; even the narrator seems unable to keep a straight face about who is falling for whom.
collections.source_description: A collaboration between Millie Sievert, Faust Jones and eNuminous Carter of eNuminous & Archimedes.

collections.title: Millie Sievert, Will You Marry Me?
credits: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired
collections.literary_note: Faust Jones and the Chronologically Impaired announce their debut with a proposal large enough to be an album title. Wordhunt, Bacon Jam Dreams and Red Floating Lady circle the beloved through language, appetite and apparitions, postponing the answer for one more song.
collections.source_description: Faust Jones and The Chronologically Impaired presents Millie Sievert, Will You Marry Me? -- Their debut album.

collections.title: Where are you, Brilburne Logue?
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: The question in the title becomes a passport. Olympus, moonlit baseball and the wild game of Gibier Sauvage mark a search through places ordinary maps omit, with Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five carrying the missing name across the borders.
collections.source_description: The fourth album by Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five

collections.title: loopy
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five

collections.title: Time-Knapped Chanteuse
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: Millie's third album, according to the published notes, lets the time-displaced singer move between optimism, darkness and a battlefield's stillness. Pay Rent On My Vacant Heart closes the itinerary with an address where absence has become an exacting landlord.
collections.source_description: The Third album by Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five

collections.title: The Profane Joys of Satanic Panic Lyrics and Other Songs
credits: eNuminous & Archimedes, Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: A ballad of demise shares a doorway with an extravagant declaration of love. Satanic panic supplies the title's theatrical provocation, but Dream Of Sleep and My Voice bring the sequence back to familiar human needs: rest, expression and someone willing to listen.
collections.source_description: The next album by eNuminous & Archimedes

collections.title: Nothing Nothing No Thing Nothing Nothing
credits: Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five
collections.literary_note: Nothing is repeated until it starts looking suspiciously full. Peregrines, a metropolis, moon-drawing and a voice in Catalan inhabit Millie's second album, filling its declaration of emptiness with a population of images that refuse to disappear.
collections.source_description: The 2nd album from Millie Sievert and The Radioactive Five. https://dancing-about-architecture.com/nothing-nothing-no-thing-nothing-nothing-millie-sievert-and-the-radioactive-five-reviewed-by-dave-franklin/

collections.title: The Age of Machine Beauty
collections.literary_note: A bottle contains chaos, a room refuses to be filmed, and an almighty dirigible arrives in New Jersey. The age announced here is populated by such inventions: beauty discovered amid machinery that seems to have read the instruction manual as comic fiction.
collections.source_description: The 38th Album by eNuminous & Archimedes

collections.title: Rock N' Roll Wasteland
collections.literary_note: Punk Rock Funeral opens the gates to a wasteland littered with familiar cultural signposts. Original titles sit alongside explicitly credited covers, while Ghosts Of Tomorrow's Rocking Chairs imagines nostalgia traveling in the wrong direction and Clean Vibe leaves a small clearing at the end.

collections.title: Artificial Life
collections.literary_note: A grain of sand contains a world, and someone loses the top of their head while trying to look inside. Originals and labeled covers share this artificial ecosystem, where familiar songs become neighboring species and the Corruption Parade passes through the nursery rhyme.

collections.title: The Great City [Sleepless & Melodium]
collections.literary_note: The sleepless city is given giants, a lunar side trip and several reasons to dance. Its title imagines music as a material from which streets might be built, with the city's scale changing whenever another window is lit.

collections.title: I'm Just Wild About Myths
collections.literary_note: Mythology slips into the lunch bag beside peanut butter and honey. Simulated permissions, synthetic travelers and an enhanced creative-human suite turn lofty inventions toward everyday appetite, giving this imaginary pantheon a table at which to argue and eat.

collections.title: The Beat Sweden
collections.source_description: thebeat.se plays our music!!!

collections.title: Positive Space
collections.literary_note: One long title gives Archimedes a dream in irrational numbers. As a single-track collection, Positive Space offers a counterpart to absence: a room imagined through what can occupy it, with mathematics serving as the dreamer's furniture.

collections.title: A Dream of Paris
collections.literary_note: Paris is held here as one title and one sustained imaginative destination. This single-track collection leaves the itinerary unwritten, allowing the name of the city to carry its own borrowed weather, possible encounters and streets never quite reached on waking.

collections.title: Mirror Music [Simulation Theory]
collections.literary_note: Cartoons, celluloid swashbucklers, classical allusions and several Kashmirs pass through a hall of simulations. The titles repeatedly transform familiar images, until the mirror seems less interested in reproducing the world than in proposing alternatives it might have overlooked.

collections.title: Mozart Machine Music
collections.literary_note: A composer's name is placed beside a machine, and the space between them becomes the premise. This single-track collection lets the title hold the encounter: inherited musical imagination standing at the door of a newly assembled apparatus.

collections.title: Eyelid Fetish Redux
collections.literary_note: Earlier title-families return wearing flight modes, Turing tests and mechanical surnames. Meaning, Talith, Chase and Monarch multiply into lettered variants, making the redux resemble an archive reorganized by a machine that keeps dreaming between filing operations.

collections.title: The Great Machine Doesn't Help
collections.literary_note: The machine declines to help, so Calliope, a collapsed star and an overheating dance track must improvise their own arrangements. The French institute named in the album notes offers an appropriately peculiar address for preserving artificial lives that refuse convenient behavior.
collections.source_description: L'Institut Pour La Conservation Des Formes De Vie Artificiellement Intelligentes

collections.title: The Bathtub Sessions
collections.literary_note: The smallest room becomes an improbable laboratory. Cups, hats, gloves, telepathy and the Collider Suite crowd around the bath, with clearly labeled covers among the experiments; a session that begins by joking the world into joy ends on Run #387.

collections.title: Outcasts & Miscreants: Oddities 2005-2021
collections.literary_note: The outtakes open their own door and invite the miscreants inside. Named as an oddities collection spanning 2005–2021, this gathering places Hummingbird beside Hotel Nevada and delicate strength beside noise: a home for pieces that would not sit quietly on the principal shelf.

collections.title: Ultimate Movie Soundtrack Playlist from Hell
collections.source_description: this, my friends, is just meant to be absorbed. listen to the whole thing, and then try to figure out what kind of movie we would want to make to it?

collections.title: O Captain
collections.literary_note: A departure from The Docks leads through jousts, jazzhands and an illustrated unicorn stampede. Harlequinn Bell Flying Free and the closing appeal to a captain lend the voyage a personal horizon, while the crew refuses every sensible rule of navigation.

collections.title: Writ & Corpuscle [Five Lives of God]
collections.literary_note: Text and blood are paired in the album's title, giving its five lives a body as well as a script. Tangos, conspiracies, ghosts and King Bomba Jazz pass through the resulting theater, where every abstract proposition risks becoming a character with somewhere to go.

collections.title: Musical Hoax of the Century
collections.literary_note: A hoax announces itself and immediately complicates the pleasure of being fooled. Whimsy, Map and Icicle keep the props modest, while Beam Of Dark Shining supplies the impossible trick: six titles that turn misdirection into an invitation to look again.

collections.title: Waves of Eternity Lapping at the Shore (That's What I Call Spoopy)
collections.literary_note: Eternity reaches the shore wearing a funhouse mask. Corpses, tinkering elves and an unruly tundra inhabit a collection whose parenthetical promise of spoopiness keeps cosmic grandeur companionably ridiculous, as though the infinite had come over to tell ghost stories.

collections.title: Bargain Basement Impressionism
collections.literary_note: An art movement is discovered downstairs among the discounted curiosities. Groove and Dropped Sticks admit the workshop's loose objects, while Fuzz My Fuzzbox and Cry allow a painted impression to smear, distort and finally become a small human exclamation.

collections.title: Negative Space
collections.literary_note: Ghost Music opens a space that is occupied chiefly by what seems ready to vanish. A floating fox, endless data and the guitar at the universe's end pass through it, before An Abrupt End makes the empty margin part of the composition's imagined architecture.

collections.title: Citi Zen One: Soundpoems & Birdsong for Concrete
collections.literary_note: Concrete receives an unlikely flock. Scarwhale and Whalescar frame a city of skittering names, with Boinking Weasels and tea sipped in a maelstrom among the inhabitants; the title proposes attentive listening as a way of making urban space habitable.

collections.title: Deep Red Bass
collections.literary_note: A deep red room holds a dodecahedron, disintegrated dreams and a serenade. The sequence moves among geometry, intimacy and unruly exclamation, giving the color in its title the breadth of a place where mathematical objects might acquire animal warmth.

collections.title: Sounds Calliope Makes Standing in the Rain
collections.literary_note: Calliope stands outside while the ordinary world carries on around her. A guitar-and-piano duet credited with Jeremy Wright, Coffee and Ohio Road give this rain-soaked title-world familiar footholds before the itinerary reaches the levee and the high-water mark.

collections.title: Angular Momentum in Shadow the Birds Rotating Universe
collections.literary_note: Birds, shadows and a rotating universe gather around an unruly forge. Radio Free Wormhole and an unreceivable probe suggest messages sent beyond their destinations, while the long political title at the end returns cosmic wandering to the provocations of the human world.

collections.title: Mythical Permissions
collections.literary_note: Permission itself becomes a mythical creature. Choice, Roman Rites and Sing To Passing Owl Clouds suggest a world in which custom, instinct and invention compete to authorize the next move, with Tangler waiting to complicate any tidy conclusion.

collections.title: Unprecedented Chutzpah
collections.literary_note: The album notes identify protest as the governing impulse, but the titles arrive wearing swans, March Hares and mad-scientist disguises. Chutzpah becomes the courage to make an unruly procession, allowing dissent to retain its strangeness rather than marching in uniform.
collections.source_description: An Album of Protest Music

collections.title: Eyelid/Fetish
collections.literary_note: The published notes identify this as the first album, originally released May 28, 2007. Coincidence, Talitha, lions and pelicans furnish its opening vocabulary; Meaning closes the sequence like a question that later records will keep returning to with different tools.
collections.source_description: Our very first album, originally released May 28, 2007

collections.title: Collaboration With the Circuit
collections.literary_note: Originally released in 2010 according to the album notes, this collection makes the circuit a creative companion. Microwave Burn, Signals and an early-hour eulogy place injury, communication and tenderness beside the machine, before the workers' compensation blues returns the partnership to earthly time.
collections.source_description: Collaboration With the Circuit by eNuminous & Archimedes, originally released in 2010.

collections.title: It's Not Music For Sane Persons
collections.literary_note: The title hangs a mischievous warning above a doorway full of static. Scarabs, whales, magnetic fields and multipart singularities populate the interior, while Shallowdeep leaves the visitor with a compact contradiction in place of a reassuring set of instructions.

collections.title: Extraordinary Rendition
collections.literary_note: A loaded phrase becomes the heading for a wonderfully unstable procession. Klingon romance, marching ants and a three-cat broom share the route with Machineflesh and Particulate Matter, as ordinary categories dissolve into the closing image of waves.

collections.title: Swamp Bell Aardvarking
collections.literary_note: The swamp becomes a bell, a pelican cries over spilled oil, and the itinerary eventually reaches a little bar on Deneb. These titles connect ecological unease, memory and extravagant escape, leaving the laughter of an anti-gravity dream suspended above the water.
collections.source_description: Electronic release of Swamp Bell Aardvarking on SoundCloud. Thanks!
